{{Short description|Graph drawing with vertices on a circle}}
[[File:Chvatal Lombardi.svg|thumb|Circular layout of the [[Chvátal graph]]]]
[[File:BGP FSM 3.svg|thumb|Circular layout of a [[state diagram]] for the [[border gateway protocol]]]]
[[File:Barabasi Albert model.gif|thumb|upright=1.2|Incremental construction of a circular layout for the [[Barabási–Albert model]] of social network formation]]
In [[graph drawing]], a '''circular layout''' is a style of drawing that places the [[vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] of a [[graph theory|graph]] on a [[circle]], often evenly spaced so that they form the vertices of a [[regular polygon]].

==Applications==
Circular layouts are a good fit for communications [[Network topology|network topologies]] such as [[Star network|star]] or [[ring network]]s,<ref>{{harvtxt|Doğrusöz|Madden|Madden|1997}}.</ref>  and for the cyclic parts of [[metabolic network]]s.<ref>{{harvtxt|Becker|Rojas|2001}}.</ref> For graphs with a known [[Hamiltonian cycle]], a circular layout allows the cycle to be depicted as the circle, and in this way circular layouts form the basis of the [[LCF notation]] for Hamiltonian [[cubic graph]]s.<ref>{{harvtxt|Pisanski|Servatius|2013}}.</ref>

A circular layout may be used on its own for an entire graph drawing, but it also may be used as the layout for smaller clusters of vertices within a larger graph drawing, such as its [[biconnected component]]s,<ref>{{harvtxt|Doğrusöz|Madden|Madden|1997}}; {{harvtxt|Six|Tollis|1999b}}.</ref> clusters of [[gene]]s in a gene interaction graph,<ref>{{harvtxt|Symeonidis|Tollis|2004}}.</ref> or natural subgroups within a [[social network]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Krebs|1996}}.</ref> If multiple vertex circles are used in this way, other methods such as [[force-directed graph drawing]] may be used to arrange the clusters.<ref>{{harvtxt|Doğrusöz|Belviranli|Dilek|2012}}.</ref>

One advantage of a circular layout in some of these applications, such as [[bioinformatic]]s or social network visualization, is its neutrality:<ref>{{harvtxt|Iragne|Nikolski|Mathieu|Auber|2005}}.</ref> by placing all vertices at equal distances from each other and from the center of the drawing, none is given a privileged position, countering the tendency of viewers to perceive more centrally located nodes as being more important.<ref>{{harvtxt|Huang|Hong|Eades|2007}}.</ref>

==Edge style==
The edges of the drawing may be depicted as [[Chord (geometry)|chords]] of the circle,<ref>{{harvtxt|Six|Tollis|1999a}}.</ref> as circular arcs<ref name="lombardi"/> (possibly perpendicular to the vertex circle, so that the edges model lines of the [[Poincaré disk model]] of [[hyperbolic geometry]]), or as other types of curve.<ref name="gk07">{{harvtxt|Gansner|Koren|2007}}.</ref>

The visual distinction between the inside and the outside of the vertex circle in a circular layout may be used to separate two different styles of edge drawing. For instance, a circular drawing algorithm of {{harvtxt|Gansner|Koren|2007}} uses edge bundling within the circle, together with some edges that are not bundled, drawn outside the circle.<ref name="gk07"/>

For circular layouts of [[regular graph]]s, with edges drawn both inside and outside as [[Arc (geometry)|circular arcs]], the [[angle of incidence (optics)|angle of incidence]] of one of these arcs with the vertex circle is the same at both ends of the arc, a property that simplifies the optimization of the [[Angular resolution (graph drawing)|angular resolution]] of the drawing.<ref name="lombardi">{{harvtxt|Duncan|Eppstein|Goodrich|Kobourov|2012}}.</ref>

==Number of crossings==
Several authors have studied the problem of finding a [[permutation]] of the vertices of a circular layout that minimizes the [[crossing number (graph theory)|number of edge crossings]] when all edges are drawn inside the vertex circle. This number of crossings is zero only for [[outerplanar graph]]s.<ref>{{harvtxt|Six|Tollis|1999a}}; {{harvtxt|Baur|Brandes|2005}}.</ref> For other graphs, it may be optimized or reduced separately for each [[biconnected component]] of the graph before combining the solutions, as these components may be drawn so that they do not interact.<ref>{{harvtxt|Baur|Brandes|2005}}.</ref> In general, minimizing the number of crossings is [[NP-complete]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Masuda|Kashiwabara|Nakajima|Fujisawa|1987}}.</ref>

{{harvtxt|Shahrokhi|Sýkora|Székely|Vrt'o|1995}} described an [[approximation algorithm]] based on [[Cut (graph theory)|balanced cuts]] or edge separators, subsets of few edges whose removal disconnects the given graph into two subgraphs with approximately equal numbers of vertices. After finding an approximate cut, their algorithm arranges the two subgraphs on each side of the cut recursively, without considering the additional crossings formed by the edges that cross the cut. They prove that the number of crossings occurring in the resulting layout, on a graph <math>G</math> with <math>n</math> vertices, is
<math display=block>O\Bigl(\bigl(\rho\log n\bigr)^2\cdot\bigl(C+\sum_{v\in V(G)}\deg(v)^2\bigr)\Bigr),</math>
where <math>C</math> is the optimal number of crossings and <math>\rho</math> is the approximation ratio of the balanced cut algorithm used by this layout method.{{sfnp|Shahrokhi|Sýkora|Székely|Vrt'o|1995}} Their work cites a paper by [[Fan Chung]] and [[Shing-Tung Yau]] from 1994 that claimed <math>\rho=O(1)</math>, but this was later found to have an erroneous proof.{{sfnp|Shmoys|1997}} Instead, the best approximation known for the balanced cut problem has <math>\rho=O(\sqrt{\log n})</math>,{{sfnp|Arora|Rao|Vazirani|2009}} giving this circular layout algorithm an [[approximation ratio]] of <math>O(\log^3 n)</math> on graphs that have a large number of crossings relative to their [[degree (graph theory)|vertex degrees]].

Heuristic methods for reducing the crossing complexity have also been devised, based e.g. on a careful vertex insertion order and on [[Local search (optimization)|local optimization]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Mäkinen|1988}}; {{harvtxt|Doğrusöz|Madden|Madden|1997}}; {{harvtxt|Six|Tollis|1999a}}; {{harvtxt|He|Sýkora|2004}}; {{harvtxt|Baur|Brandes|2005}}.</ref> A circular layout may also be used to maximize the number of crossings. In particular, choosing a [[random permutation]] for the vertices causes each possible crossing to occur with probability 1/3, so the [[expected value|expected number]] of crossings is within a factor of three of the maximum number of crossings among all possible layouts.  [[Derandomization|Derandomizing]] this method gives a [[Deterministic algorithm|deterministic]] [[approximation algorithm]] with [[approximation ratio]] three.<ref>{{harvtxt|Verbitsky|2008}}.</ref>

==Other optimization criteria==
Along with crossings, circular versions of problems of optimizing the lengths of edges in a circular layout, the angular resolution of the crossings, or the [[cutwidth]] (the maximum number of edges that connects one arc of the circle to the opposite arc) have also been considered,<ref>{{harvtxt|Mäkinen|1988}}; {{harvtxt|Gansner|Koren|2007}}; {{harvtxt|Nguyen|Eades|Hong|Huang|2011}}; {{harvtxt|Dehkordi|Nguyen|Eades|Hong|2013}}.</ref> but many of these problems are NP-complete.<ref>{{harvtxt|Mäkinen|1988}}.</ref>

==See also==
*[[Chord diagram (information visualization)]], a closely related concept in information visualization
*[[Planarity]], a puzzle in which a player must move vertices to untangle a drawing of a [[planar graph]], starting from a randomized circular layout
